content: Azulene is an organic compound composed of molecules containing 10 carbon atoms and 8 hydrogen atoms. Its structure consists of a five-membered ring fused to a seven-membered ring. Azulene is classified as a monoterpene. It is an isomer of naphthalene, but its physical properties differ significantly. While naphthalene appears as a white crystalline solid, azulene is a dark blue crystalline solid. The name azulene is derived from the Spanish word azul, meaning blue. Azulene is widely used in various cosmetic products. Historically, azulene has been known since the 15th century as the azure-blue distillate obtained through steam distillation of chamomile. The compound was formally discovered and named in 1863 by Septimus Piesse, who identified it in azure-blue distillates from other sources such as yarrow and wormwood. The structural elucidation of azulene was achieved by Lavoslav Ružička, and its first organic synthesis was carried out in 1937 by Placidus Plattner. Derivatives Vetivazulene, also known as 4,8-dimethyl-2-isopropylazulene, is derived from vetiver oil. Another derivative, guaiazulene (1,4-dimethyl-7-isopropylazulene), occurs naturally as a component of guaiac wood oil. Structure Azulene's structure consists of a fused cyclopentadiene ring and a cycloheptatriene ring, making it an isomer of naphthalene. It is a 10 π-electron system, similar to cyclodecapentaene, and exhibits aromatic properties despite not being a single-ring system like benzene. The peripheral bonds in azulene have comparable lengths, with the exception of the shared bond in the middle, which is a single bond. The aromatic stability of azulene is approximately half that of naphthalene. The molecule can be conceptualized as a fusion of a 6 π-electron aromatic cyclopentadienyl anion and a 6 π-electron aromatic tropylium cation. This interpretation is supported by its dipole moment of 0 Debye. Organic Synthesis For many years, synthetic routes to azulene were limited, making the compound expensive to produce. A more recent synthetic approach uses cycloheptatriene as the starting material. In naphthazulenes, a naphthalene ring is fused with the 1,2-position of an azulene ring. In one such system, deformation from planarity is observed, resembling the structural distortion seen in tetrahelicene.
